parts.title: My grandmother's camera
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When my grandmother died last spring, my mother gave me her old camera. It is a heavy metal one from the 1970s, and at first I did not know what to do with it. It uses film, which you have to buy in small rolls, and you cannot see the picture until it has been developed.

I took it to a photography shop in town, where an old man showed me how to load the film. 'Think before you press the button,' he told me. 'You only have thirty-six pictures, so each one must count.' That was very different from my phone, on which I take hundreds of pictures a day and delete most of them.

I spent a week photographing my street, my friends and my little brother. When I collected the pictures, I was surprised. Some were blurry, and one was only a finger, but several were beautiful, with soft colours that no phone could give. My mother cried when she saw a photograph of our dog sleeping, because it looked just like an old family picture.

Now I carry the camera everywhere. I take fewer pictures than before, but I look at the world more carefully, and I feel closer to my grandmother.

options: To think before taking a picture

questions.explanation: She takes fewer pictures but looks at the world more carefully.

parts.title: Taking better photographs
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Many people think that you need an expensive camera to take good photographs, but this is not true. [1] The following tips will help you take better pictures with any camera, even a phone.

First, think about the light. The best time to take photographs is early in the morning or just before sunset, when the light is soft and golden. [2] In the middle of the day, the sun is high and can make faces look hard and shadowy.

Second, get closer to your subject. Beginners often stand too far away, so the person looks tiny. [3] If you are photographing a friend, try to fill the picture with their face.

Third, look at the background before you press the button. [4] A tree growing out of someone's head is one of the most common mistakes! Moving one step to the side can solve the problem.

Finally, do not be afraid to take many photographs. [5] Nobody becomes an expert without making mistakes, so keep practising.
sentences: Sometimes there is something strange behind your subject.
My brother likes to take photographs of birds.
Many beautiful pictures are taken with very simple cameras.
You can always delete the ones that you do not like.
Photographs taken then often look warm and magical.
This makes the details clearer and the picture more interesting.

gaps.explanation: "This is not true" is followed by evidence that simple cameras can produce beautiful pictures.
"Taken then" refers to early morning or sunset, when the light is soft and golden.
"This" refers to getting closer, which shows details; the example with a friend's face follows.
The strange thing behind the subject leads to the example of a tree growing out of a head.
"The ones you do not like" refers to the many photographs that you take.

parts.title: Photo competition rules
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Welcome to the Young Photographers' Competition! Anyone [1] is between ten and sixteen years old can enter. You may send up to three photographs, but they must all be [2] by you. Each photograph must show something that you can find [3] your town. Please do not change the pictures on a computer. The winner [4] receive a new camera. All entries must arrive [5] the end of June. If you have any questions, please ask your teacher [6] email us.

gaps.explanation: A relative word is needed to describe "Anyone".
"Taken by you" means that you took the photographs.
Something that you can find "in" your town.
"Will receive" is a promise about the future.
"By the end of June" gives a final date.
"Or" shows a choice between asking the teacher and emailing.

parts.title: A photography workshop
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: sylvester
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to today's photography workshop. We'll start at the park gate at ten o'clock and finish at one. First, I'll show you how to hold your camera properly. Use both hands, and keep your elbows close to your body. Then we'll practise taking pictures of flowers near the lake. After a break for lunch, we'll try photographing moving things, such as birds. Don't worry if your photos are blurry at first. At the end, we'll choose the three best photographs, and the winner gets a book about photography. The workshop costs fifteen pounds. Please wear comfortable shoes, because we'll walk about three kilometres altogether.

parts.title: A travel photographer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: My guest today is Marlon Dacey, a travel photographer. Marlon, how did you pay for your first camera?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: I was fourteen, and I delivered newspapers every morning for eight months. It was a secondhand camera, but I thought it was the most beautiful thing in the world.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: Has anything ever gone badly wrong?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: Yes. In Peru, I dropped my camera into a river and lost six hundred pictures. I sat on the bank for an hour and nearly gave up.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: Which is your favourite country to photograph?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: Iceland. The light changes every few minutes, so you can stand in one place and take twenty completely different pictures.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: What makes a good photograph?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: It tells a story. You look at it and wonder what happened before and what will happen next. The colours matter less than people think.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: What advice would you give to a beginner?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: Print your photographs. On a screen, you glance and move on, but a printed picture makes you look properly.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: And what comes next for you?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: I'm having an exhibition in London next year, with pictures from twenty years of travelling.
